questions.question: When are two norms $\|\cdot\|_p$ and $\|\cdot\|_q$ on $\boldsymbol{V}$ called equivalent?
options: When $a\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p\leq\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q\leq b\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$ for all $\boldsymbol{v}$, with $a,b>0$ depending on $\boldsymbol{v}$.
When $a\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p\leq\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q\leq b\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$ for some $a,b>0$ and all $\boldsymbol{v}$.
When $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q\leq b\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$ for some $b>0$ and all $\boldsymbol{v}$.
When $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p=\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q$ for every $\boldsymbol{v}\in\boldsymbol{V}$.

questions.question: What role do the constants $a$ and $b$ play in norm equivalence?
options: Fixed positive constants working for every vector.
They depend on the individual vector, with no fixed positive pair working for every vector.
They must both be equal to $0$.
They are vectors in $\boldsymbol{V}$.

questions.question: If $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q = 2\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$ for every $\boldsymbol{v}$, which constants show equivalence?
Which pair is an example of equivalent norms?
options: The discrete metric and a $p$-metric
The empty norm and the zero function
The radius of convergence and interval length
The Euclidean norm and the taxicab norm

questions.question: What is true for finite-dimensional vector spaces?
options: Any two norms on a finite-dimensional vector space are equivalent
Two distinct norms on a finite-dimensional vector space are not equivalent
Only identical norms can be equivalent
Norm equivalence is defined only for infinite-dimensional spaces

questions.question: What is the interpretation of equivalent norms?
options: They agree on which vectors have length at most $1$.
Their ratio $\|v\|_q/\|v\|_p$ is one constant for all $v\ne0$.
Their lengths are comparable up to fixed scaling factors.
One of them is at least as large as the other for every vector.

questions.question: Suppose $\frac{1}{2}\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p\leq\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q \leq 3\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$. If $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p = 4$, what range is guaranteed for $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q$?
options: $4\leq\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q \leq 12$
$0\leq\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q \leq 3$
$\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q = 4$
$2\leq\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q \leq 12$

questions.question: Let $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q = \frac{1}{3}\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$ for every $\boldsymbol{v}$. What constants $a$ and $b$ prove equivalence?
Which assumption is essential for the equivalence-of-norms theorem that any two norms are equivalent?
options: The vector space has no zero vector
The constants are allowed to be negative
The norms are defined only for one vector
The vector space is finite-dimensional

questions.question: Why would constants depending on $\boldsymbol{v}$ not prove equivalence as defined?
options: Constants depending on $\boldsymbol{v}$ may be negative, but $a,b$ must be positive
The definition requires fixed constants working for every $\boldsymbol{v}\in\boldsymbol{V}$
With $\boldsymbol{v}$-dependent constants the bounds would fail at $\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{0}$
Such constants only exist when $\boldsymbol{V}$ is finite-dimensional

questions.question: If $a\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p\leq\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q\leq b\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$ with $a,b \gt 0$, which reverse comparison follows?
options: $\frac{1}{b}\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q\leq\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p\leq\frac{1}{a}\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q$
$b\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q\leq\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p\leq a\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q$
$\frac{1}{a}\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q\leq\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p\leq\frac{1}{b}\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q$
$a\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q\leq\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p\leq b\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q$

questions.question: Suppose only $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q\leq 5\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$ is known for every $\boldsymbol{v}$. Is this alone enough to prove equivalence?
options: Yes, dividing by $5$ gives the reverse bound $\frac{1}{5}\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q\le\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$
Yes, every norm already has the lower bound $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q\geq 0$
No, because the upper constant $b=5$ would have to be at most $1$ as well
No, a lower bound $a\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p\leq\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q$ with $a>0$ is also needed

questions.question: For equivalent norms, what must be true of the constants $a$ and $b$?
options: They are positive but may be chosen separately for each $\boldsymbol{v}$.
They must be equal, $a=b$, and independent of the vector.
They may be any nonnegative numbers, so $a=0$ is allowed.
They are positive and independent of $\boldsymbol{v}$.

questions.question: What is the informal meaning of equivalent norms?
options: They give exactly the same value for every vector.
They differ by at most a fixed additive constant on every vector.
They measure length comparably up to fixed scaling factors.
One of them bounds the other from above by a fixed factor.

questions.question: What does the lower inequality $a\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p\le \|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q$ prevent?
options: $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q$ from being too large vs $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$.
$\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q$ from differing from $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$.
$\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q$ from ever dropping below $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$.
$\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q$ from being too small vs $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$.

questions.question: If $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q=\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$ for every $\boldsymbol{v}$, which constants prove equivalence?
If $2\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p\le\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q\le5\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$ for every $\boldsymbol{v}$, what follows?
options: The two norms cannot be equivalent.
$\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$ is not a norm.
$\boldsymbol{v}$ must be zero.
The two norms are equivalent.

questions.question: On a finite-dimensional vector space, what can be concluded about any two norms?
options: They are equivalent.
They are never equivalent.
They must be exactly equal.
They must both be Euclidean norms.

questions.question: Why is a one-sided inequality not enough to prove norm equivalence?
options: Equivalence needs two fixed bounds, each controlling the other.
A one-sided bound only controls vectors in the unit ball of $\|\cdot\|_p$.
Equivalence needs the two norms to agree on some nonzero vector.
Equivalence needs bounds with constant $1$ in both directions.

questions.question: If $\frac{1}{4}\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p\le\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q\le4\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$ and $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p=3$, what bounds follow for $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q$?
options: $\frac{1}{12}\le\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q\le\frac{4}{3}$
$\frac{1}{4}\le\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q\le4$
$\frac{3}{4}\le\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q\le12$
$\frac{3}{4}\le\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q\le4$
